constraints: Claims are annotated to source spans.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: For uncited exploratory brainstorming with no deadline, grounding and usable-output gates could be relaxed to diagnostic measures.
details.errorCorrection: Fluency, first-token speed, average time, and cost do not establish that the answer is supported or usable within the contract.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends grounding factual answers in direct source text and verifying claims with citations; the p95 and validation thresholds are scenario-defined service rules.
details.scenarioApplication: Block release when a cited proposition lacks a retrieved span or when validated completion misses the p95 deadline, while tracking spend separately.

messages.text: Fluency and first-token speed can hide unsupported claims and a late invalid final answer.
Averages conceal tail behavior, and qualitative citation review is too late for a release gate.
Cost is relevant but cannot prove that retrieved evidence supports the answer.
A supported source span is required for each material cited proposition.

feedback.reason: Source support and usable end-to-end time are independent release constraints; either a plausible answer or a fast partial response can still fail.

options.text: Use fluency and time to first token as the launch gate, then review citations after release.
Require each material claim to have support in the retrieved source span.
Use average completion time and defer citation support to a qualitative audit.
Gate on p95 time to a complete, validated answer, including the citation check.
Choose the lowest-cost route and treat grounding as a model preference.

prompt: A legal research assistant answers from retrieved case excerpts. A response can sound plausible, but release depends on whether each cited proposition is supported by the retrieved passage and whether the answer arrives within the analyst’s deadline. Select TWO release measures.

constraints: The payment token is sensitive even when the ticket is resolved.
The aggregate completion and satisfaction measures miss the failure.
A deterministic output check and a safety evaluation slice can be added.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If review found only harmless style variation with no privacy or safety impact, completion and satisfaction could remain primary while style is monitored.
details.errorCorrection: More complaints, data deletion, or temperature changes do not make the privacy failure measurable or acceptable.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic says success criteria should be specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant to user needs, including safety and privacy; deterministic checks are a scenario-appropriate implementation.
details.scenarioApplication: Add a payment-token detector and reviewed privacy slice, gate release on it, and continue reporting completion so a quality improvement cannot hide a safety regression.
details.transfer: Promote every consequential production harm into a visible criterion while preserving the outcome measures that still matter.

messages.text: Waiting leaves the known disclosure outside the release contract and adds no detection.
Removing sensitive cases removes the risk signal instead of controlling it.
Temperature is not a substitute for a privacy criterion or a detector for a literal token.

feedback.reason: The audit exposes a high-severity outcome that the aggregate metric does not represent, so privacy must become an explicit criterion without discarding useful task measurement.

options.text: Keep the headline completion metric and wait for a larger sample of customer complaints.
Add a privacy/safety gate and redaction check while retaining task completion.
Delete cases containing payment data so the completion score reflects ordinary support work.
Lower temperature and treat the existing completion score as evidence that the assistant is safe.

prompt: A support assistant reports 96% task completion and high satisfaction, but a weekly audit finds a customer payment token in an otherwise correct reply. Latency and cost remain within budget. What should the team do first?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A correct handoff still has a cost; report handoff rate and resolution time so product owners can assess the tradeoff.
details.errorCorrection: Do not reward unsupported confidence or hide all abstentions from the denominator.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Evaluation metrics should operationalize the user outcome, including appropriate abstention and downstream handling.
details.scenarioApplication: Label whether each case was answerable, whether the answer was supported, and whether an unanswerable case was correctly routed; report coverage and conditional accuracy alongside the primary resolved-task metric.
details.transfer: Make the success metric match the complete completion contract, not a convenient proxy.

messages.text: Answer rate rewards unsupported answers even when the requirement explicitly values safe withholding and handoff.
Conditional accuracy hides coverage and whether the system correctly handed off cases it could not support.
Response length does not measure supported resolution or whether abstention was appropriate.

feedback.reason: The product requirement defines success as a supported answer or a correct handoff when evidence is insufficient. Evaluate that full resolution contract rather than answer rate alone.

options.text: Raw answer rate, because a system should answer as often as possible.
Count supported answers and correct handoffs as distinct successes.
Accuracy only among answered questions, with abstentions excluded from every metric.
Average response length, because shorter abstentions are cheaper.

prompt: A model answers directly in 82% of cases and abstains in 18%. Audits show that direct answers are correct in 96% of answered cases, while the product requirement says unsupported cases must be withheld and a correct handoff counts as success. Which metric best evaluates the requirement?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If no additional sample were possible, the owner would need to apply the existing uncertainty policy rather than assume a pass.
details.errorCorrection: Do not treat a favorable point estimate as certainty or move a threshold after seeing uncertainty.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A point estimate and uncertainty interval answer different questions; the release rule determines which evidence is sufficient.
details.scenarioApplication: Continue evaluation on the same target population and adjudication method, then report the updated estimate and interval against the 93% gate.
details.transfer: Set the acceptance rule and evidence requirement before the outcome, then use uncertainty to decide whether more data are needed.

messages.text: The estimate is uncertain and the prespecified interval includes materially below-threshold performance.
Changing the acceptance threshold after observing the interval changes the release contract.
Combining versions does not add independent candidate evidence and answers a different question.

feedback.reason: The point estimate clears the gate, but the prespecified interval does not establish that the candidate reliably meets it. Use the available larger sample under the same protocol.

options.text: Approve because the point estimate is above 93%.
Lower the gate to the interval midpoint so the current sample is decisive.
The interval does not establish that the prespecified gate passes.
Average the candidate’s score with the prior model’s result to shrink the interval.

prompt: A release gate requires at least 93% accuracy on the adjudicated target population. A candidate’s observed accuracy is 94% on 50 cases, but the prespecified 95% confidence interval is 88%–98%; a larger evaluation can be completed before launch. What should the release owner do?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Resolve labels or report the uncertainty and apply the existing gate before declaring a pass.
details.errorCorrection: A high aggregate among answered cases cannot establish a high-risk release gate when that slice is unresolved.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Success may include a supported answer or an appropriate handoff, but each outcome should be visible under the release contract.
details.scenarioApplication: Unlabeled cases are unknown, not automatically successes or failures.

messages.text: The criterion recognizes supported handoffs as outcomes distinct from failure, and the high-risk evidence gap still limits the gate.
Category counts help, but imputing missing high-risk outcomes does not establish observed release performance.
A nonsignificant rate change does not remove outcome categories or resolve the missing high-risk labels.

feedback.reason: The answered-only rate omits material workflow outcomes and a high-risk slice has unresolved labels. A release claim needs a predeclared outcome definition and valid subgroup evidence.

options.text: The answered-case result is encouraging but incomplete; report abstention and handoff outcomes separately and resolve or bound the high-risk slice before the gate.
Use 97% among answered cases as the primary gate, disclose the abstention and handoff rate, and let the adjudicated three quarters support the high-risk pass while labels remain pending.
Count abstentions by policy category and impute the high-risk unlabeled quarter from the adjudicated cases in the same release.
Compare answer accuracy among completed cases and report abstention and handoff rates only if either differs significantly.

prompt: A release report shows 97% success among answered cases. Another 9% of the eligible requests were abstained or handed off, and a high-risk subgroup has unresolved labels for a quarter of its cases. Which release conclusion is supported?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Complete or explicitly bound the missing evidence before declaring the existing gate passed.
details.errorCorrection: A sufficient aggregate sample does not establish performance on an incompletely measured high-risk slice.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Define success across the supported answer and handoff paths while keeping outcome rates visible.
details.scenarioApplication: Unadjudicated labels are unknown, not successes or failures by default.
details.transfer: Report both the overall outcome and the slices that can change release risk.

messages.text: A caveat does not make the partial score sufficient for the stated outcome contract or resolve the high-risk evidence gap.
An accepted handoff may need its own outcome definition, and imputing missing labels does not establish the subgroup result.
The scenario asks what can be claimed for the release; excluding a required high-risk slice needs an explicit scope decision, not an implicit pass.

feedback.reason: The report omits an intended workflow outcome and has incomplete evidence for a high-risk slice. A headline score cannot establish the release criterion under those omissions.

options.text: Publish 97% as the primary answer-quality estimate, report the 9% abstention or handoff rate separately, and let the high-risk pass stand until its labels are complete.
Count handoffs as success when the handoff was accepted, and impute the remaining high-risk labels from the completed half.
The completed-answer score is partial evidence; report the handoff outcomes and bound or finish the high-risk slice before a release claim.
Release to the lower-risk population now and defer the high-risk population until its labels are complete.

prompt: A release score is 97% across completed answers. The required outcome also counts an appropriate handoff as success; 12% of requests were handed off, and the report excludes them. A high-risk slice has only half its labels adjudicated. What can be claimed?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Preserve the release criterion and report the uncertainty if the needed sample is not yet available.
details.errorCorrection: Translated labels do not turn English model behavior into observed Spanish outcomes.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Aggregate stability does not establish performance for a required subgroup.
details.scenarioApplication: Use valid cases from the relevant language and risk slice, with a denominator sufficient for the declared threshold.

messages.text: Eight high-risk Spanish cases do not establish the required per-language safety floor, even with the sampling breakdown shown.
Translated examples are not observed Spanish model outcomes and cannot represent language-specific behavior.
The release criterion already requires a per-language floor; insufficient evidence means the floor is unverified, not removable.

feedback.reason: The sample is not representative of production and has too few high-risk Spanish observations to establish its separate safety floor.

options.text: Reweight the 400-case estimate to production’s 40% Spanish mix and shrink the small high-risk Spanish estimate toward English outcomes, while flagging its uncertainty.
Rebalance or supplement the evaluation to represent production language mix and obtain enough valid high-risk Spanish cases for its separate floor.
Translate the English prompts and reference labels, then add those translated cases to the Spanish denominator.
Use a single safety floor across languages until the Spanish sample reaches the same size as English.

prompt: A task-quality report shows the required score on 400 reviewed cases, but the sampling log shows 240 were routine English requests and only 8 were high-risk Spanish requests. constraints: Labels are adjudicated and slice confusion matrices are available.
A missed high-risk case has documented impact.
The false-negative ceiling and recall floor are release rules for this service.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If classes had equal consequence and balanced volume, an overall accuracy threshold could be a reasonable primary gate.
details.errorCorrection: Post-release monitoring, volume weighting, and a model swap leave the stated slice boundary without a release veto.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends success criteria that are measurable and relevant to user needs, including safety; the false-negative ceiling is a scenario policy.
details.scenarioApplication: Reject the release when the high-risk slice exceeds its ceiling, while publishing overall and per-slice results for context.
details.transfer: Give an explicitly harmful subgroup its own measurable release boundary when aggregate performance can hide that harm.

messages.text: A later dashboard does not prevent release of a slice that already exceeds its safety boundary.
Volume weighting makes rare high-impact errors less visible rather than controlling them.
A larger model may change accuracy but does not define or enforce the required slice gate.

feedback.reason: The high-risk slice has a release-blocking error boundary that an aggregate accuracy score can conceal, so it needs its own gate.

options.text: Set a high-risk false-negative ceiling or recall floor beside overall and per-slice accuracy.
Ship once overall accuracy clears the target and add the high-risk slice to a post-release dashboard.
Weight every class by volume so the largest slice determines the release score.
Replace the classifier with a larger model without changing the release metric.

prompt: A fraud classifier reports 94% overall accuracy, but a small high-risk slice has four times the false-negative rate of ordinary cases. The release committee must define its metric gate. Which action is best?

constraints: The team has adjudicated labels and an error-cost model.
High-value claims have separate safety and service limits.
The twenty-to-one loss ratio is a documented scenario premise.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If all errors had equal consequences and reviewer capacity were unconstrained, macro-F1 could be sufficient for comparison.
details.errorCorrection: Macro-F1, average precision, and token volume do not reflect the asymmetric business consequence or guarantee high-value escalation quality.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends multidimensional criteria such as task fidelity, privacy, latency, and price; the loss model and reviewer capacity are scenario inputs.
details.scenarioApplication: Calculate expected loss using adjudicated error costs, inspect high-value slices, and reject any release that breaches a hard safety or service limit.
details.transfer: Align evaluation weights with the consequence of each error, while keeping non-negotiable ceilings outside the composite score.

messages.text: Macro-F1 treats a twenty-fold miss and a low-cost false positive too similarly for this route.
Average precision still omits the stated cost asymmetry and high-value safety boundary.
Token use does not measure the twenty-to-one error cost or show whether high-value escalations are missed.

feedback.reason: A twenty-fold error-cost difference makes equal-weight macro-F1 an incomplete decision metric; hard limits must remain constraints rather than being averaged away.

options.text: Choose the release with the higher macro-F1 because equal class weighting is easiest to explain.
Compare only average precision and let reviewers absorb any change in high-value misses.
Use cost-weighted expected loss plus per-class results; retain hard safety and service limits.
Choose the release with lower token use and accept the same macro-F1, assuming cheaper inference leaves more reviewer capacity for high-value misses.

prompt: A claims router has similar macro-F1 for two releases, but a missed high-value escalation costs twenty times a false positive and reviewer capacity is fixed. Which comparison should guide the release?

constraints: The case inventory, abstentions, adjudicated labels, and high-risk slice can be enumerated; the release committee needs a metric contract before comparing versions.

details.errorCorrection: Excluded abstentions and an unrepresented consequential slice can make the model appear safer and prevent a defensible comparison now. The competing action therefore leaves the stated decision boundary unresolved.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic lists task fidelity, privacy preservation, latency, and price as separate criteria and recommends multidimensional evaluation. The case-specific population, thresholds, roles, and authority limits are supplied by this scenario rather than by the provider documentation.

details.transfer: Make the measured population and every material failure boundary explicit before comparing versions.

messages.text: Deferring the high-risk slice permits an invalid headline score to authorize a release.
A composite number still cannot repair an unknown population or guarantee that a consequential slice is represented.
Removing abstentions hides a material outcome and makes the routine denominator look more complete than it is.
Required control: Define the eligible denominator, count abstentions explicitly, and publish a prespecified high-risk slice with adjudicated labels.
Required control: Keep fidelity, safety and privacy, latency, and price as separate gates, and block release until the comparable rerun is complete.

options.text: Keep the 98% score as the primary release measure and add the high-risk slice in the next evaluation cycle.
Define the eligible denominator, count abstentions explicitly, and publish a prespecified high-risk slice with adjudicated labels.
Replace the invalid accuracy score with one cost-weighted utility number and proceed while its denominator is still unresolved.
Keep fidelity, safety and privacy, latency, and price as separate gates, and block release until the comparable rerun is complete.
Drop abstentions from both versions and compare routine-case accuracy while monitoring the high-risk path after rollout.

prompt: A claims model reports 98% accuracy, but the score excludes abstentions and contains labels only for routine claims. The new release adds a high-risk claim path whose outcomes are not in the denominator. Select TWO: Which controls are required before the release comparison?

constraints: The two metric definitions, evaluator versions, case IDs, refusal counts, and run dates are available; no immutable metric version is attached to the dashboard comparison.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If R2 and R3 used the same immutable evaluator definition and population, the existing accuracy/safety/latency/cost gates could compare the releases directly.
details.errorCorrection: Rerun both releases under one frozen, newest evaluator definition before comparing them; relabeling historical R2/R3 scores without rerunning cannot establish equivalence and would imply an improvement the data do not measure.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic says success criteria should be specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant to user needs, including safety and privacy concerns. The case-specific population, thresholds, roles, and authority limits are supplied by this scenario rather than by the provider documentation.

details.transfer: Version the measure, its population, and its owner whenever new evidence changes a lifecycle decision.

messages.text: Post-hoc normalization cannot establish equivalence between changed labels and refusal rules.

Relabeling historical scores does not make results from different evaluator versions comparable. Preserve the original evaluator metadata and rerun both releases on the same frozen cases with the same evaluator version.

options.text: Split the dashboard by metric and evaluator version, rerun comparable cases under one frozen definition, and report refusals separately.
Normalize the two scores after the fact and keep the combined trend so the release decision is not delayed.
Relabel the historical R2 and R3 scores with the newest evaluator version without rerunning the cases.

prompt: Release R3 appears to improve accuracy over R2, but the evaluator changed its label taxonomy and excluded a new refusal class midway through the measurement period. Both versions are shown on one dashboard line. Select TWO: Which actions make this comparison decision-ready?

constraints: Eligibility facts have a reviewed reference.
Privacy failures are more severe than stylistic imperfections.
The latency and cost limits are release commitments.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: For a non-sensitive offline summarizer with no latency or cost commitment, fidelity could carry more of the release decision, but that is a different contract.
details.errorCorrection: Helpfulness and public benchmarks omit the service data and hard boundaries, while response length is only an indirect signal.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic presents task fidelity, privacy, latency, and price as distinct success criteria; the thresholds and reviewed slices are policy decisions supplied by this scenario.
details.scenarioApplication: The team should score the summary against the adjudicated record, run privacy checks, calculate p95 latency, and attribute spend per case before launch.
details.transfer: When several failure dimensions matter, keep them as explicit measures and gates instead of hiding them inside one headline score.

messages.text: Helpfulness does not test eligibility fidelity or provide a veto for a severe privacy failure.
A public benchmark does not represent this document distribution or the service operating envelope.
A composite score can let a severe privacy, tail-latency, or spend breach be offset by gains elsewhere; those boundaries need independent gates.

feedback.reason: Separate release measures are needed because the service can satisfy one dimension while violating another, and privacy, tail latency, and spend are explicit boundaries.

options.text: Use caseworker helpfulness as the sole launch metric and review privacy complaints after release.
Choose the model with the highest public benchmark, compare its aggregate score on a few cases, and track average latency during rollout.
Set separate fidelity, privacy/safety, p95 latency, and per-case cost gates on representative slices.
Use one calibrated utility score combining fidelity, privacy, p95 latency, and cost, then ship when its aggregate clears target.

prompt: A public benefits service summarizes applicant documents for caseworkers. It must preserve adjudicated eligibility facts, protect unrelated personal data, meet a 3-second p95 target, and stay within a per-case budget. Which evaluation contract should govern launch?

constraints: Traces record time to first token, final token, validation completion, and p95 usable completion.
The output must pass JSON validation before the user can act.
The streaming choice is for an interactive request.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If users could act on free-form tokens and no final validation existed, first-token time could be the primary responsiveness measure.
details.errorCorrection: First-token, average final-token, or validation-only metrics each omit a stage that determines whether the itinerary can be used.

details.scenarioApplication: Calculate p95 from request start through final token and JSON validation, and retain first-token timing to diagnose perceived responsiveness.
details.transfer: Define latency at the point the consumer can safely use the result, then keep earlier milestones as diagnostics.

messages.text: A fast partial token does not make an itinerary actionable or valid.

Validation-only timing ignores model and transport time before validation can begin.

feedback.reason: The consumer’s usable response begins only after the complete payload passes validation, so first-token timing is useful context but not the service promise.

options.text: Use time to first token as the sole responsiveness SLO because it captures perceived speed.
Use average time to final token and ignore validation because validation is application work.
Measure only validation duration and optimize it independently of model completion.

prompt: A consumer chat UI streams a reassuring first token quickly, but users cannot act until a validated JSON itinerary is complete; final validation occasionally adds two seconds. Which latency measure should drive the service contract?
